subject: Python
scope: This map takes a learner from no Python to training and evaluating scikit-learn models on their own data. It follows the order most Python-for-data-science courses use and the scientific Python stack itself is built on: core Python first, then NumPy, then pandas and plotting, then machine learning with scikit-learn. Core Python is covered in full because reading library code, error messages and documentation needs it. That includes a short topic on classes, because scikit-learn's estimators are objects with methods and fitted attributes. NumPy and pandas cover loading, cleaning, reshaping and exploring data. The machine learning part follows scikit-learn's own organisation: the estimator API, preprocessing and pipelines, supervised models, evaluation, model selection, ensembles and a little unsupervised learning, with concepts like overfitting and data leakage taught where the code needs them. Left out: deep learning frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow), the mathematical derivations behind the algorithms, web development, async, concurrency, packaging and publishing libraries, type hints and testing frameworks, and big-data tools. These are worth learning later but are not needed for the stated goal. Seaborn and other plotting libraries are left out in favour of matplotlib and pandas plotting, which are enough for exploring data.

profile.name: Python
profile.trap: a = [1, 2]; b = a; b.append(3); print(a) prints [1, 2, 3], even though the code never touched a. Assignment in Python never copies anything. It makes a name refer to an object, so a and b are two names for the same list, and changing the list through one name shows through the other. The same rule explains why a function can change a list you pass to it, and why a pandas DataFrame or NumPy slice you 'copied' with = changes the original.
profile.slips: Forgetting the colon after an if or for line, typing pirnt instead of print, a missing closing parenthesis, writing from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegresion, or misspelling a column name like df['prcie'].
profile.observe: Run the code and print things: type(x) and id(x) show what an object is and whether two names share it, a is b tests sameness, and help(obj) or dir(obj) lists what it can do. For data, print df.shape, df.dtypes, df.head() and df.isna().sum() after every step. For models, print the fitted attributes such as model.coef_ or model.classes_. The key habit is to change one thing, run it again and compare the output.
profile.rich: You are given a small DataFrame of houses with a price column, a size column that has some missing values and a text column for the neighbourhood. Split the data into training and test sets, build a pipeline that fills the missing sizes and one-hot encodes the neighbourhood, fit a linear regression, and print the test-set mean absolute error. Then explain why the imputer has to sit inside the pipeline and not be applied before the split.
profile.examples: Short, complete programs that run on their own, each followed by its exact output. Data is built in the code as a tiny list, array or DataFrame, never read from an outside file, and random_state is fixed so a model's printed numbers are the same on every run.

topics.name: Getting Started
topics.desc: How to run Python code and see its results, the first step before anything else can be tried.
points: Running code: scripts, the REPL and notebooks

topics.name: Basic Types
topics.desc: The built-in kinds of values (numbers, text, truth values) and how to convert between them, since every program is built from them.

topics.name: Control Flow
topics.desc: Making decisions and repeating work, which together decide the order a program's statements run in.

topics.name: Collections
topics.desc: Python's built-in containers for many values, and the shared rules for indexing, iterating over and changing them.

topics.name: Functions
topics.desc: Packaging code into reusable named pieces with inputs and outputs, and how names are looked up inside them.

topics.name: Errors and Debugging
topics.desc: Reading what went wrong, handling failures in code, and finding bugs, the skills used every time code does not work.
points: Common exceptions: TypeError, KeyError, IndexError, ValueError

topics.name: Modules and Packages
topics.desc: Using code from the standard library, installed packages and your own files, and keeping project dependencies separate.
points: Useful standard library modules: math, random, collections

topics.name: Working with Files
topics.desc: Getting data into and out of a program through files, which is where real datasets come from.
points: Reading and writing text files with open() and with
Reading CSV and JSON with the standard library

topics.name: Classes and Objects
topics.desc: How objects bundle data with behaviour, the model behind every library object you use, including scikit-learn estimators.
points: Defining a class with __init__ and self
Duck typing: objects that share an interface

topics.name: Iteration in Depth
topics.desc: What a for loop really does underneath, and how to produce values lazily.

topics.name: NumPy Arrays
topics.desc: The array, the fixed-type grid of numbers that pandas and scikit-learn store data in, and how to pick out parts of it.

topics.name: Array Computation
topics.desc: Computing on whole arrays at once instead of looping, which is how numerical Python is fast and how ML code is written.

topics.name: pandas Fundamentals
topics.desc: Loading tabular data into a DataFrame, looking at it and selecting the parts you need.
points: Selecting rows with loc and iloc

topics.name: Cleaning Data
topics.desc: Finding and fixing the problems real datasets have before they can be analysed or modelled.
points: Dropping and filling missing values in pandas
Fixing column types with astype and to_numeric

topics.name: Reshaping and Combining Data
topics.desc: Summarising, joining and restructuring tables to get data into the shape a question or model needs.
points: apply and when to avoid it

topics.name: Visualizing Data
topics.desc: Plotting data to understand distributions and relationships before modelling and to check results after.
points: Line and scatter plots with matplotlib

topics.name: Machine Learning Concepts
topics.desc: The ideas every model rests on: what is being learned, from what, and how to tell whether it learned anything useful.
points: What a model learns: features, target and parameters
Overfitting, underfitting and the bias-variance tradeoff

topics.name: The scikit-learn API
topics.desc: The shared interface all scikit-learn objects follow, so learning it once lets you use any model.
points: The feature matrix X and target y
Hyperparameters versus fitted attributes (the trailing underscore)

topics.name: Preprocessing and Pipelines
topics.desc: Turning cleaned data into model-ready numbers inside scikit-learn so the same steps apply to training and new data without leakage.
points: Imputing missing values in a model with SimpleImputer

topics.name: Regression Models
topics.desc: Predicting numbers, starting with linear models whose workings can be read directly from their coefficients.
points: Regression metrics: MAE, MSE, RMSE and R²

topics.name: Classification Models
topics.desc: Predicting categories with the standard families of classifiers and understanding how each draws its boundary.

topics.name: Evaluating Classifiers
topics.desc: Measuring how good a classifier really is, beyond a single accuracy number.
points: Accuracy and its limits on imbalanced data

topics.name: Model Selection and Tuning
topics.desc: Comparing models and choosing hyperparameters with reliable estimates, while keeping a fair final test.
points: Choosing a splitter: KFold, StratifiedKFold and GroupKFold
Keeping a final test set untouched

topics.name: Ensemble Models
topics.desc: Combining many trees into stronger models, which are the usual best choice for tabular data.

topics.name: Unsupervised Learning
topics.desc: Finding structure in data with no target, for exploration and for building features.
points: Choosing the number of clusters: inertia and silhouette

topics.name: Completing a Project
topics.desc: Putting everything together into a full workflow and keeping the result, so the learner can work on their own data.
points: An end-to-end ML workflow from CSV to evaluated model
Saving and loading models with joblib
